c1.t: FIJENSE SI PARA  LA INTRO VA MEJOR  Copper (Cu), is an essential micronutrient for humans,animals, plants and microrganisms and  it participates in various morphological, physiological, and biochemical processes. However, excessive Cu are harmful to plants. High levels of copper can cause chlorosis, reduce photosynthesis, alter nutrient absorption, and decrease plant biomass. (Ferrol et al. 2016; Nazir et al. 2019).  One of the adaptive strategies that plants have developed to colonize sites with high concentrations of heavy metals, such as Cu, is the association with soil microorganisms, in particular with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AM) (Miransari 2011; Ferrol et al. 2016). The average abundance of Cu in the earth’s crust is 60 mg Cu kg 1 (Lide, 2009) and concentrations in soil vary between 2 and 50 mg kg 1 (Alloway, 2012). c0.t: Si queremos poner la onda en seguridad alimentarias Safe Intake Limits: EFSA established a new acceptable daily intake (ADI) for copper of 0.07 mg/kg of body weight, updated from earlier higher levels. For an adult, this equates to a safe limit of approximately 5 mg per day. Food Contamination & Sources: Copper is considered a micronutrient but can become a contaminant. Sources contributing to total dietary copper include natural presence in food, pesticide usage, and food additive
